front: What was the impact of Presidential Reconstruction on African American rights?
p1: Johnson issued mass pardons to Southern whites → Confederate land returned → '40 acres and a mule' never realised.
p2: Black Codes introduced by Southern states → restricted movement, labour and property rights → de facto re-enslavement.
p3: Johnson vetoed the Civil Rights Act (1866) and Freedmen's Bureau bill → Congress overruled him.

front: What were the key achievements of Radical Reconstruction?
p1: 14th Amendment (1868) → citizenship + equal protection. 15th Amendment (1870) → voting rights for Black men.
p2: Reconstruction Act (1867) → South divided into military districts → Black Codes removed → elections enforced.
p3: 1,500+ African Americans held public office → 22 in Congress, including Hiram Revels, first Black senator.

front: Why did Reconstruction fail?
p1: Hayes–Tilden Compromise (1877) → federal troops withdrawn → 'Redeemer' governments retook the South.
p2: Deaths of Sumner and Stevens + Panic of 1873 → Northern attention shifts → Radical Republican majority diluted.
p3: 1873 Supreme Court ruling in the Slaughterhouse Case → civil rights ruled a state issue → undermined 14th Amendment.

front: What was the impact of the Freedmen's Bureau?
p1: Established 1865 → helped create 1,000+ Black schools → 250,000 enrolled → founded Howard University (1867).
p2: Distributed 21 million rations of food to freedmen → provided basic housing, medical care and legal support.
p3: Closure of the Bureau in 1872 → gains immediately reversed without federal infrastructure to sustain them.

front: What was the impact of KKK terror during Reconstruction?
p1: KKK founded in Tennessee (1865) by Nathan Bedford Forrest → violence used to stop African Americans voting, learning and asserting rights.
p2: Colfax Massacre (1873): c.100 African Americans killed in Louisiana after contested elections → federal government failed to help. Memphis and New Orleans Riots (1866): dozens to 200 killed.
p3: Grant passed the Enforcement Acts (1870-71) → first KKK suppressed, over 600 prosecuted → resurgent and unpunished after 1877 troop withdrawal.

front: Why did sharecropping trap African Americans in poverty?
p1: No land redistribution after emancipation → '40 acres and a mule' never realised → freedpeople stayed on the same land under the same landowners.
p2: Crop-lien system → sharecroppers paid rent in crops → always in debt to landowner → effective debt bondage.
p3: By 1900 only 25% of African Americans owned land → economic freedom impossible without land ownership.

front: What was the impact of Jim Crow laws on African Americans?
p1: Spread across the South from 1877 → segregated schools, transport, hospitals, parks, restaurants and churches.
p2: Black schools systematically underfunded → worsening economic opportunity.
p3: All-black towns and districts gave an economic alternative, e.g. Greenwood in Tulsa or Mound Bayou.

front: What was the significance of the Wilmington Coup (1898)?
p1: White supremacists violently overthrew the biracial elected government of Wilmington, North Carolina (1898).
p2: Showed that even legitimate political power could be destroyed by organised white violence without federal protection.
p3: Mississippi v Williams (1898) → Supreme Court ruled voter suppression did not violate the 15th Amendment → over 90% disenfranchised by 1900.

front: What was the significance of Booker T. Washington?
p1: Atlanta Compromise (1895): accepted social segregation in exchange for economic co-operation with whites → founded Tuskegee Institute (1881).
p2: Negro Business League (1900): 600 chapters → promoted a parallel Black economy → secretly funded legal challenges to disenfranchisement.
p3: Trusted adviser to President Roosevelt → secured federal appointments for Black Americans → criticised by Du Bois and Trotter for conceding political and social rights.

front: What were the criticisms of Booker T. Washington's Atlanta Compromise?
p1: Du Bois argued the Compromise sacrificed political and social rights → accommodation legitimised segregation.
p2: William Monroe Trotter: Washington's autocratic control of Black organisations stifled debate → Wilmington Coup (1898) showed accommodation failed to protect Black communities.
p3: Niagara Movement (1905): Du Bois launched an immediate alternative demanding full civil rights → Washington's strategy left most African Americans in poverty.

front: What was the impact of lynching on African American social rights?
p1: Lynching epidemic → 100+ per year in early 1890s → tool of racial terror to enforce social hierarchy and deter political participation.
p2: Ida B. Wells published 'Southern Horrors' (1892) → documented frequency, disproved the myth it answered violent crime → national + international campaign.
p3: Southern Democrats repeatedly defeated anti-lynching bills in Congress → Governor Tillman of South Carolina openly defended lynching (1900).

front: What was the impact of convict leasing on African Americans?
p1: Exploited 13th Amendment loophole ('except as punishment for crime') → trivial arrests of African Americans → leased to private companies.
p2: Grew across the South in the 1880s → effectively recreated slavery → dangerous conditions, no pay, no rights.
p3: System designed to control the Black population and provide cheap labour to Southern economies → continued into the early 20th century.

front: What ideas and attitudes were used to justify Jim Crow?
p1: Lost Cause myth: United Daughters of the Confederacy romanticised slavery and framed the Civil War as a states' rights struggle → Confederate monuments erected.
p2: Social Darwinism: framed African Americans as inferior → eugenic theories seen as modern science → racial separation justified as natural order.
p3: Religious justification: 'God almighty drew the colour line' (Richmond Times editor) → churches actively supported segregation.

front: What evidence is there of Black economic success during the Gilded Age?
p1: Tuskegee Institute (1881): Washington trained artisans and professionals → 50,000 Black professionals by 1900, including doctors, lawyers and teachers.
p2: Parallel economy: barbershops, undertakers and small shops formed the basis of a Black middle class → over 50,000 Black-owned businesses by the 1890s.
p3: Du Bois: first Black Harvard PhD (1895) → BUT gains fragile: convict leasing and crop-lien system kept most in poverty.

front: How different were AA experiences outside the South in the Gilded Age?
p1: North → better jobs + education, growing Black middle class → BUT de facto segregation: NY Harlem a separate district for 23,000
p2: West → relative racial indifference → Bass Reeves: Deputy US Marshal who arrested thousands → all-Black towns like Allensworth, California allowed self-governance
p3: Limits → Exoduster movement (1879): 40,000 fled South to Kansas → faced hostility + hardship.

front: What were the key Supreme Court cases during the Gilded Age?
p1: Plessy v Ferguson (1896): Homer Plessy's challenge to segregation on trains rejected → 'Separate but equal' established. 8-1 decision.
p2: Mississippi v Williams (1898): SC upheld literacy tests and poll taxes → legitimised voter suppression across the South.
p3: Cumming v Board of Education (1899): unanimous decision that racial segregation could extend into schools.

front: How did state governments hinder Black rights in the Gilded Age?
p1: After 1877 Democratic Redeemer governments regained control → swept away Reconstruction rights and introduced Jim Crow laws.
p2: Voter suppression: Mississippi (1890) → literacy tests, poll taxes, grandfather clauses → Black voter registration fell from 90% (1867) to 6% (1892).
p3: State governments took no action on racial violence → Governor Tillman of South Carolina openly defended lynching (1900).

front: Why did Southern elites introduce voter suppression in the Gilded Age?
p1: Populist Party threat: in 1892 Populists won 5 states and 8.5% of the vote → threatened to divide the white vote.
p2: Economic control: disenfranchisement kept African Americans dependent on white landowners as sharecroppers → racial hierarchy underpinned the plantation economy.
p3: Black officeholders, e.g. Wilmington NC, provoked a violent white supremacist backlash.

front: How was voter suppression implemented in the Gilded Age?
p1: Literacy tests: voters had to interpret complex constitutional clauses → administered subjectively against Black voters → Mississippi registration fell from 90% (1867) to under 6% by 1900.
p2: Poll taxes kept impoverished sharecroppers from the ballot → grandfather clauses exempted men whose ancestors voted before 1867, excluding Black voters.
p3: Violence and intimidation: Wilmington Coup (1898), when a white mob overthrew a biracial government.

front: What was the strategy and significance of the NAACP?
p1: Founded 1909 by Du Bois, Ida B. Wells + white progressives → legal litigation + political pressure → The Crisis magazine reached 100,000 readers by 1918.
p2: Legal challenges: overturned grandfather clauses (US v Guinn, 1915) → challenged lynching → campaigned for federal anti-lynching legislation blocked by Southern Democrats.
p3: Membership grew to 500,000 → presence in North and South → limited impact on Southern Jim Crow in this period.

front: What was the significance of Marcus Garvey and UNIA?
p1: UNIA New York branch (1917) → The Negro World: 200,000 weekly readers → promoted Black pride, self-reliance and Pan-Africanism.
p2: Black Star Line (1919): Black-owned steamship company → Back to Africa movement → mass appeal to urban Black Americans disillusioned with racism.
p3: Decline: met the KKK (1922) → convicted of mail fraud → deported to Jamaica (1927) → UNIA collapsed, but influence persisted in NOI and later Black nationalism.

front: What was the significance of Birth of a Nation and the second KKK?
p1: Birth of a Nation (1915): Griffith film glorified the KKK, depicted Black men as violent sexual predators → screened at the White House by Wilson, who praised it → led directly to KKK revival.
p2: Second KKK: 5 million members by the 1920s, 15% of population → national, not just Southern → included politicians, police chiefs and judges across North and West.
p3: 1925: Klan burned crosses outside NAACP offices → KKK members in public office undermined law enforcement → showed white supremacy was national, not uniquely Southern.

front: What was the impact of WWI on African Americans?
p1: 380,000 African Americans served in segregated units → 369th 'Harlem Hellfighters' fought under French command → less racial segregation in Europe.
p2: Great Migration: around 2 million African Americans moved from the South to northern and western cities by 1940 seeking industrial work.
p3: Post-war violence: Red Summer of 1919 → race riots in Chicago (38 killed) and over 30 cities → Elaine Massacre: 200+ Black sharecroppers killed in Arkansas for organising.

front: How far did black political rights develop in the 1920s?
p1: Most African Americans remained in the South, where voter suppression was embedded → removal of grandfather clauses (US v Guinn, 1915) achieved little.
p2: NAACP membership surged in Northern cities → Northern Black voting blocs created political power.
p3: Oscar De Priest elected first Northern Black congressman (Chicago, 1928) → BUT de facto segregation and racial violence persisted in the North.

front: What was the significance of the Great Migration?
p1: Great Migration (1916 onwards): African Americans moved from the rural South to Northern and Western cities → escaping Jim Crow + seeking industrial jobs → WWI phase: 500,000 moved 1916-19
p2: Created influential Black urban communities in Harlem and South Side Chicago → fostered cultural and political movements → NAACP membership surged in Northern cities
p3: Economic shift: 40% of Black men in North held skilled jobs by 1920 vs 15% in South → BUT de facto segregation, housing covenants and hostility persisted

front: What was the significance of W.E.B. Du Bois?
p1: First Black Harvard PhD (1895) → Niagara Movement (1905) demanded full civil rights immediately → co-founded NAACP (1909).
p2: The Souls of Black Folk (1903): articulated 'double consciousness', Black Americans torn between American and racial identity → The Crisis magazine reached 100,000 readers.
p3: Critique of Washington: Atlanta Compromise conceded too much → advocated the 'Talented Tenth', an educated Black leadership → under FBI surveillance, labelled a communist threat.

front: What was the significance of the Harlem Renaissance?
p1: 1920s cultural explosion → Langston Hughes, Louis Armstrong, Zora Neale Hurston → Black artistic achievement gained national recognition.
p2: Harlem population grew 50,000 → 200,000 (1910–1930) → Du Bois used The Crisis to promote Black intellectualism.
p3: Cultural flourishing did not bring political or economic gains → KKK at 5 million same decade → Tulsa (1921) destroyed 'Black Wall Street'.

front: What was the impact of the Tulsa Race Massacre (1921)?
p1: White mob destroyed Greenwood District ('Black Wall Street') → 600+ Black-owned businesses destroyed → 35 blocks burned.
p2: Up to 300 African Americans killed → 10,000 left homeless → one of the worst incidents of racial violence in US history.
p3: Showed that Black economic success provoked violent white backlash → prosperity offered no protection without political and legal rights.

front: What was the impact of the Great Depression on African Americans?
p1: Black unemployment 50% vs 25% national → 'last hired, first fired' → sharecroppers worst hit, 75% of Southern African Americans still in agriculture.
p2: AFL excluded Black workers → confined to menial jobs → Depression wiped out Great Migration gains in the North.
p3: 50+ African Americans lynched annually in late 1920s → NOI (1930) offered Black nationalist dignity and self-reliance → Father Divine's Peace Mission fed thousands free.

front: What was the New Deal's impact on African American political rights?
p1: FDR created informal 'Black Cabinet' → led by Mary McLeod Bethune → influenced New Deal programmes for Black Americans.
p2: Eleanor Roosevelt advocated civil rights + supported anti-lynching bills → symbolic gestures like resigning from the DAR.
p3: African Americans began voting Democratic in large numbers → 3/4 voted Republican in 1932, 3/4 Democrat in 1936.

front: How did the First New Deal affect African Americans economically?
p1: FERA → provided direct relief → 20–30% of recipients African American → CCC employed c.200,000 African Americans (10% of enrolment).
p2: Some Black sharecroppers became independent farmers through federal assistance → Black Cabinet influenced programme delivery.
p3: AAA (1933) displaced 200,000 Black sharecroppers → NRA codes manipulated by employers → gains partial and uneven.

front: How did the Second New Deal affect African Americans?
p1: WPA → infrastructure jobs → 15% of workers African American → Social Security Act: pensions + unemployment insurance for the first time.
p2: Wagner Act (1935) → BSCP became first Black union to win AFL recognition → BUT 'closed shops' let white-only unions dominate.
p3: Bethune's role in NYA → funded training + jobs for 600,000 Black youths → most direct targeted benefit for African Americans.

front: What were the economic limitations of the New Deal for African Americans?
p1: Social Security excluded agricultural + domestic workers → 65% of Black workers → most significant exclusion from New Deal protection.
p2: Aid administered by Southern states → whites controlled distribution → African Americans discriminated against in relief policies.
p3: Anti-Communist Red Scare → organisations advocating Black economic rights suspected of communism → CIO lost funding → unions weakened.

front: How strong was the position of African Americans by 1932?
p1: Progress: literacy 10% (1865) → 85% (1930) → 300,000 in Northern schools → NAACP won US v Guinn (1915) removing grandfather clauses → Great Migration created Harlem Renaissance.
p2: Weakness: only 2% registered to vote in South → 75% still sharecroppers → Black unemployment 50% vs 25% national (Depression) → KKK 15% of eligible population.
p3: Structural limits: anti-lynching bills repeatedly blocked → Reconstruction gains fully reversed in South → NAACP legal successes but no political power.

front: Was Roosevelt's administration an effective supporter of African American rights?
p1: Effective: Black Cabinet led by Bethune → William H. Hastie first Black federal judge (1937) → Eleanor Roosevelt resigned DAR to support Marian Anderson (1939)
p2: ¾ AA voted Republican 1932 → ¾ Democrat 1936, a fundamental realignment of Black voters → WPA employed 1 million+ AA by 1939
p3: Ineffective: refused anti-lynching bill to keep Southern Democrats → AAA displaced 200,000 Black sharecroppers → Social Security excluded 65% of Black workers

front: How did state governments resist desegregation in the 1950s and 60s?
p1: States' rights ideology: Southern governors argued states should manage affairs without federal interference → massive resistance to Brown (1954) → Southern Manifesto signed by 101 congressmen.
p2: Orval Faubus (Arkansas, 1957): National Guard blocked Little Rock Nine → Eisenhower sent 101st Airborne → federal power required to enforce desegregation.
p3: Ole Miss Riot (1962): Governor Ross Barnett tried to block James Meredith's enrolment → Kennedy sent 30,000 troops to restore order.

front: What was the impact of Brown v Board of Education (1954)?
p1: Built on Gaines v Canada (1938) → Thurgood Marshall showed Southern states spent $43/yr on Black students vs $179 on white → NAACP challenged 'separate but equal'.
p2: Supreme Court unanimous: school segregation unconstitutional → overturned Plessy v Ferguson (1896) → desegregation 'with all deliberate speed' (Brown II, 1955).
p3: Impact limited by massive resistance → 1% of Southern Black children in integrated schools by 1957 → BUT galvanised the civil rights movement.

front: What was the impact of WWII on African Americans?
p1: Over 1 million African Americans served in segregated units → those stationed in Britain saw a society without Jim Crow → Tuskegee Airmen proved combat skill.
p2: Randolph's threatened March on Washington pressured FDR into Executive Order 8802 (1941), banning discrimination in defence industries.
p3: NAACP launched the Double V Campaign (victory abroad and at home) → membership grew from 50,000 to 500,000.

front: What was the impact of the Emmett Till case (1955)?
p1: Emmett Till (1955): 14-year-old from Chicago accused of whistling at a white woman → abducted, tortured, shot, thrown in Tallahatchie River.
p2: Mother Mamie Till insisted on an open casket → 50,000+ viewed the body, Jet magazine published photographs → murderers acquitted in 67 minutes.
p3: Acquitted men later confessed in magazine interview → outrage helped launch the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

front: How did the Cold War help advance civil rights?
p1: Soviet propaganda publicised US racial violence to discredit America internationally → Birmingham Campaign broadcast globally.
p2: Federal government increasingly conscious of Cold War optics → Kennedy after Birmingham: 'land of the free, except for the negroes?'
p3: Decolonisation: Gandhi's non-violent resistance inspired King's philosophy → Kwame Nkrumah's Ghana independence (1957) inspired Pan-African consciousness.

front: What were the post-war economic challenges facing African Americans?
p1: GI Bill (1944): education, housing loans and job training for veterans → but administered locally in the South.
p2: Automation hit African Americans concentrated in low-skill manual jobs → Black unemployment double white → eliminated jobs were those gained in the Great Migration and WWII.
p3: Residential segregation in the North and West compounded economic exclusion → returning veterans who asserted rights were targeted.

front: What was the role of anti-civil rights groups in the 1950s/60s?
p1: White Citizens' Council (1954): formed after Brown v Board, the "Uptown Klan" → used economic pressure, not open violence: fired workers, refused loans, evicted tenants.
p2: KKK revival: 16th Street Baptist Church bombing (1963), four girls killed, no convictions.
p3: Lynching persisted as a tool of terror → around 3,500 African Americans lynched 1882–1968, often after false accusations.

front: What was the significance of the Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955–56)?
p1: 381-day boycott by 40,000 Black residents of Montgomery, sparked by Rosa Parks' arrest and led by a young Martin Luther King.
p2: Cost the bus company $3,000 a day in lost fares → the economic pressure that forced desegregation, alongside Browder v Gayle.
p3: Launched King as the movement's leading figure → template for later non-violent mass campaigns.

front: What was the significance of the Warren Court (1953–1969)?
p1: Considered the most liberal Supreme Court in US history → transformed federal protection of civil rights through judicial activism.
p2: Brown v Board (1954) overturned Plessy: 'separate but equal' unconstitutional in education → Brown II (1955): desegregation 'with all deliberate speed'.
p3: Browder v Gayle (1956): segregated buses unconstitutional → Boynton v Virginia (1960): segregation on interstate buses unconstitutional.

front: What was the strategy and significance of the SCLC?
p1: Founded 1957 → led by Martin Luther King → strategy was non-violent direct action → used media + moral pressure to force federal response.
p2: Targeted places where violent segregationist response was likely, e.g. Birmingham and Selma → resulting media coverage forced federal intervention.
p3: FBI COINTELPRO illegally infiltrated and disrupted SCLC in the 1960s → files held on 7,000 activists, including King.

front: What was the strategy and significance of SNCC?
p1: Founded 1960 → a grassroots, student-led organisation → more radical than SCLC → organised sit-ins, Freedom Rides, voter registration drives.
p2: John Lewis, SNCC chairman, led its most visible campaigns including Selma → embodied SNCC's more confrontational style compared with SCLC.
p3: 1966 under Stokely Carmichael → rejected non-violence + integration → embraced Black Power → 'Black Power' slogan coined.

front: What was the Albany Campaign (1962) and why did it fail?
p1: SCLC and King targeted Albany, Georgia → Police Chief Laurie Pritchett used non-violent policing → denied King media images of brutality.
p2: No single dramatic confrontation → national media lost interest in Albany → federal government had no reason to intervene → no legislation resulted.
p3: Key lesson: non-violent direct action only worked when it provoked visible repression on camera → shaped the Birmingham Campaign.

front: What were the sit-ins and Freedom Rides of 1960–61?
p1: Sit-ins (1960): 4 Black students sat at a 'white-only' lunch counter in Greensboro, NC → spread to 70,000 students, coordinated by SNCC → over 1,000 businesses desegregated.
p2: Freedom Rides (1961): CORE + SNCC sent Black and white activists on interstate buses into the Deep South to test Boynton v Virginia → met by violent mobs.
p3: National outrage forced JFK's administration to press the Interstate Commerce Commission to enforce bus desegregation.

front: What was the significance of the Birmingham Campaign (1963)?
p1: King + SCLC targeted Birmingham → Bull Connor used police dogs + fire hoses against peaceful protesters including children → images broadcast worldwide.
p2: Kennedy announced America faced a 'moral duty' to intervene → directly led to the Civil Rights Act (1964).
p3: 16th Street Baptist Church bombing (1963) → KKK killed four young girls → no convictions → highlighted state complicity in racial terror.

front: What was the significance of the March on Washington (1963)?
p1: 250,000 marched for jobs and freedom → King's 'I Have a Dream' speech → largest civil rights demonstration in US history.
p2: Organised by Randolph + Rustin → brought together NAACP, SCLC, SNCC, CORE, NUL → a broad coalition.
p3: Malcolm X dismissed it as a 'farce' → highlighted divisions between integrationist and nationalist wings.

front: What was the impact of the Civil Rights Act (1964)?
p1: Removed Jim Crow segregation in public places → Title VII banned employment discrimination, enforced by the EEOC.
p2: Pushed through by LBJ using the 'Johnson treatment' → most significant federal civil rights legislation since Reconstruction.
p3: Limits: did not address de facto segregation in the North → did not solve economic inequality → enforcement weak in many states.

front: What happened during the Selma March and what did it achieve?
p1: Selma: 50% Black population but only 1% of electorate → SCLC + SNCC march to expose voter suppression.
p2: Bloody Sunday: police attacked marchers led by John Lewis on the Edmund Pettus Bridge → broadcast nationwide.
p3: Led directly to the Voting Rights Act (1965) → Mississippi Black voter registration rose from 6% (1964) to 60% (1969).

front: How did the media help advance the Civil Rights Movement in the 1950s and 60s?
p1: Televised images of Bloody Sunday (1965) + Birmingham (1963) shocked international audiences → massive support for the movement.
p2: King exploited television cameras → chose Birmingham because Bull Connor guaranteed visible brutality → forced federal response.
p3: Emmett Till's open casket (1955): media images of the body spread outrage → contrast with the 19th century press, which had perpetuated stereotypes and justified lynching.

front: What was the impact of the Vietnam War on the Civil Rights Movement?
p1: African Americans disproportionately drafted → returned radicalised + disillusioned → fed the Black Power ethos of militancy.
p2: King's 'Beyond Vietnam' speech (1967) → severed relationship with LBJ → ended federal momentum on civil rights reform.
p3: Media attention shifted from civil rights marches to anti-war protests → movement lost national spotlight → Black Power filled the vacuum.

front: What was the impact of the Great Society on African Americans?
p1: Medicare and Medicaid (1965) raised Black hospital access from 25% to 75% → Food Stamps: 33% of recipients Black.
p2: War on Poverty: OEO funded community programmes → Robert Weaver became first Black Cabinet member (1966) when the new housing department (HUD) was created.
p3: Vietnam diverted funding from Great Society programmes after 1966 → Poor People's Campaign (1968) showed legal equality had not delivered economic equality.

front: What were Malcolm X's key ideas and the Nation of Islam?
p1: NOI → Black nationalism + separatism → rejected integration → 'by any means necessary' → self-defence against white supremacy.
p2: NOI grew from 400 members (1952) to 40,000 (1960) under Malcolm X → addressed Northern urban poverty King's movement neglected.
p3: Post-Hajj (1964): adopted a more inclusive vision → broke from NOI → assassinated 1965 → martyr for Black Power.

front: What were the key ideas of Stokely Carmichael and Black Power?
p1: 1966 → took over SNCC → rejected non-violence + integration → coined 'Black Power' slogan on the Meredith March.
p2: Black Power = self-determination, Black pride, economic self-sufficiency, community control, not dependence on white liberals.
p3: Alienated white allies + moderates → CORE lost white funding 1969 → weakened the cross-racial coalition behind the 1964/65 legislation.

front: Why did Black Power rise to prominence in the late 1960s?
p1: CRM failed the North → SCLC/NAACP focused on Southern desegregation, leaving urban poverty and police violence unaddressed → Malcolm X's nationalism already rooted in Northern communities.
p2: Vietnam War → African Americans disproportionately drafted → returned radicalised and disillusioned with non-violent appeals to the government sending them to fight.
p3: Long Hot Summers (1967): 150 race riots, largest in Detroit and Newark, after Watts (1965) → exposed failure of non-violence on Northern poverty and police brutality.

front: What was the negative impact of Nixon's and Reagan's policies on African Americans?
p1: Nixon's 'Law and Order' (1968) → launched the War on Drugs → disproportionately targeted Black communities → by 1992 25% of Black men in prison, on parole or probation.
p2: Reagan claimed his administration was colour blind → conservative Supreme Court appointments → fewer Black judges → clashed with Congress over civil rights legislation.
p3: Reagan (1981-89): welfare cuts deepened economic disparities for Black Americans.

front: What was the impact of the Black Panther Party's community programmes?
p1: Founded 1966 by Huey Newton and Bobby Seale → free breakfast programmes fed 20,000 children per day → 'survival programmes' addressed poverty civil rights legislation had not solved.
p2: 13 health clinics → screened thousands for sickle cell anaemia → also 60+ community schools.
p3: BPP's 10-Point Programme demanded reparations, land, full employment, decent housing → shifted agenda from legal equality to economic justice.

front: What was the impact of COINTELPRO on Black Power organisations?
p1: FBI infiltrated Black Power groups → planted informants → manufactured evidence → created internal suspicion and divisions.
p2: Fred Hampton (Black Panther leader) killed in an FBI-orchestrated raid (1969) → Panthers collapsed by 1982.
p3: Panthers never exceeded 5,000 members → COINTELPRO accelerated collapse → showed state willingness to use illegal tactics against civil rights organisations.

front: What was the impact of affirmative action on African Americans?
p1: First introduced Philadelphia 1969 → Griggs v Duke Power Co. (1971) confirmed it was constitutional → African Americans in white-collar jobs 5% (1960) → 15% (mid-1970s).
p2: Regents of University of California v Bakke (1978) → strict racial quotas ruled unconstitutional → Reagan/Bush labelled it 'reverse discrimination' → federal enforcement reduced.
p3: By 1980s 40% of African Americans middle class → but gains uneven: a 'bifurcation' with persistent ghetto poverty alongside professional success.

front: What was the cultural impact of Black Power?
p1: Black Arts Movement (1965–75): Amiri Baraka founded Black Arts Repertory Theatre → 'cultural wing of Black Power' → 500+ Black arts organisations.
p2: 500+ Black Studies programmes in universities by 1971, demanded by student activists → Afro hairstyle and dashikis as acts of political assertion.
p3: Limits: cultural gains did not bring economic or political progress → mainly felt by the middle class and educated → people in ghettos saw little change.

front: What was the Poor People's Campaign (1968) and why did it fail?
p1: Came from the failure of the Chicago Campaign (1966) → demanded $30 billion federal anti-poverty programme → multiracial coalition; King assassinated before it launched.
p2: Resurrection City: 3,000 camped on National Mall → poor conditions, internal tensions → evicted by police → Congress unmoved as Vietnam consumed attention.
p3: Legal equality had not delivered economic equality → King's economic focus alienated moderate white allies → assassination ended the attempt to unite the poor across racial lines.

front: What was the political position of African Americans by 1992?
p1: 8,000+ African Americans held public office by 1992 → Douglas Wilder first Black governor (Virginia, 1989) → Shirley Chisholm first Black woman in Congress (1968).
p2: Jesse Jackson won 7 million votes in 1984 and 1988 presidential campaigns → Congressional Black Caucus grew to 36 members.
p3: Turnout 54% vs 61% white → unofficial suppression persisted: gerrymandering, insufficient polling stations.

front: What was the significance of the Los Angeles Riots (1992)?
p1: Erupted after all-white jury acquitted LAPD officers for beating Rodney King → $1 billion of damage → 63 killed.
p2: Showed police brutality + racial injustice remained systemic → civil rights legislation had not changed realities for urban Black communities.
p3: Positive strides by 1992: Oprah, Michael Jordan, Spike Lee as icons of success → BUT persistent stereotypes + poverty for the majority.

front: What was the economic position of African Americans by 1992?
p1: African Americans earned 60% of average white income → Black unemployment 14.2% vs 6% white by 1992.
p2: Homeownership 43% vs 70% white → legacy of redlining and blockbusting, with homes resold to Black families at inflated prices.
p3: Bifurcation: 40% middle class by 1980s BUT persistent underclass in inner cities → War on Drugs disproportionately targeted Black Americans.

front: What was bussing and what was its impact?
p1: Swann v Charlotte-Mecklenburg (1971): Supreme Court upheld bussing as a constitutional remedy for school segregation → courts began ordering cross-boundary bussing.
p2: Boston Busing Crisis (1974-76): white mobs attacked school buses → white flight to suburbs accelerated.
p3: By 1980s federal courts rolled back bussing orders → by 1992, 40% of Black students in majority-Black schools: resegregation had accelerated.

front: How did the Michael Donald case (1981) end differently from earlier lynchings?
p1: 19-year-old Michael Donald murdered by Klansmen in Mobile, Alabama, a rare lynching so late in the century.
p2: Unlike historic lynchings: strong federal response, murderer found guilty and executed.
p3: Civil suit brought by the SPLC bankrupted the United Klans of Alabama.

front: What was the right to exist and collectively bargain in 1865?
p1: No legal protections for unions → courts upheld employers' right to suppress organising → 20 state governments allowed militias to intervene in labour disputes.
p2: NLU (1866): first national federation, 300,000 at peak → collapsed after Sylvis died (1869).
p3: No obligation for employers to recognise unions → KOL (1869) growing but excluded from political power → collective bargaining had no legal standing.

front: What was the right to strike in 1865?
p1: Fewer than 5% of strikes led to concessions → scab labour widespread → blacklisting common, in Pennsylvania shared among 50 mine operators.
p2: Courts issued injunctions against strikes in railroads and mining → Molly Maguires: violence demonised the labour movement → members arrested and executed.
p3: Public hostility: newspapers called strikers 'rioters' or 'anarchists' → no legal right to strike → strikes treated as criminal conspiracies restraining trade.

front: What were fair and safe working conditions in 1865?
p1: 3,000 railroad workers killed and 20,000 injured annually → children as young as 8 worked 12-hour shifts for $1/week.
p2: Female textile workers earned $3-6/week vs $7-10 for men → immigrants worked 60-70 hours/week in sweatshops for $1/day.
p3: No minimum wage, no safety legislation, no compensation for injury → no legal framework for employer-provided benefits → injured workers simply dismissed.

front: What was the significance of the Great Railroad Strike (1877)?
p1: Spontaneous nationwide strike after wage cuts in a depression → spread from West Virginia across the country → rail traffic shut down.
p2: Federal troops called in → killed over 100 workers → government focused on order, not workers' grievances.
p3: First nationwide labour dispute → exposed need for stronger organised unions → showed violent resistance was the government's default response to strikes.

front: What was the significance of the NLU and CNLU?
p1: Founded 1866 by William Sylvis → first national labour federation, 300,000 at peak.
p2: Pushed for legislative reforms including the 8-hour workday → over-reliant on Sylvis personally → collapsed after his death in 1869.
p3: NLU excluded Black workers from membership → CNLU formed separately in 1869 → short-lived, lacking the NLU's reach.

front: What was the significance of the Knights of Labor (KOL)?
p1: Founded 1869: the largest labour organisation of the late 19th century, known for inclusivity → welcomed skilled and unskilled workers, women, African Americans and immigrants.
p2: Peaked at 700,000 members (1886), far surpassing the NLU's reach.
p3: Collapsed after the Haymarket Affair (1886), tainted by association with anarchism and radicalism.

front: What was the role of racial divisions in early labour?
p1: Chinese workers arrived for railroad construction → white workers saw them as wage competitors → AFL and KOL both supported the Chinese Exclusion Act (1882).
p2: Black workers excluded from the NLU formed the CNLU (1869), which soon faded → AFL (1886) continued the exclusionary pattern.
p3: Employers used Black workers as strikebreakers during disputes → deepened mistrust between Black and white workers → undermined cross-racial solidarity.

front: What was the significance of the Haymarket Affair (1886)?
p1: Rally in Chicago demanding 8-hour workday turned violent → bomb killed 7 police officers.
p2: KOL collapsed, associated with radicalism and anarchism → AFL (1886) became the safer alternative under Gompers, focused on skilled workers only.
p3: Haymarket linked industrial unionism with anarchism in the public mind → damaged the union movement for decades.

front: What was the role of the AFL during the Gilded Age?
p1: Founded 1886 by Samuel Gompers → focused on skilled workers, pushing for higher wages, shorter workdays and better conditions through collective bargaining, not confrontation.
p2: Exclusionary by design → neglected unskilled labourers, women and most African Americans.
p3: Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) routinely used against unions as illegal restraints of trade.

front: What were working conditions like during the Gilded Age?
p1: 2,000 rail workers killed in accidents in 1889 alone → by 1900, 35,000 workplace deaths annually → no federal safety legislation or compensation.
p2: Industrial wages rose 48% ($380 to $564 a year, 1880-90) but the gender gap persisted: women earned $3-6/week vs $7-10 for men → immigrants worked 10-12 hour days.
p3: 2% of population owned 30% of wealth → no minimum wage, safety standards or union recognition.

front: What was the role of skilled/unskilled divisions in the Gilded Age?
p1: AFL under Gompers focused exclusively on skilled workers → craft unionism favoured a small elite → excluded the unskilled majority.
p2: KOL, by contrast, welcomed unskilled workers → broader base but less bargaining power → collapsed after Haymarket (1886).
p3: Pullman Strike (1894) exposed the cost: AFL refused solidarity with the ARU, which organised workers across all grades → strike failed.

front: What was the impact of the government's laissez-faire attitude in the 19th century?
p1: Government refused to regulate business or labour → no minimum wage, no safety regulation, no legal right to unionise → corporations set wages and conditions unilaterally.
p2: No antitrust enforcement → monopolies formed unchecked: Carnegie (steel), Rockefeller (oil) consolidated industries into trusts.
p3: Social Darwinism + Carnegie's 'Gospel of Wealth' → inequality framed as natural and beneficial → moral cover for not regulating.

front: What was collective bargaining and why did it matter?
p1: Collective bargaining: workers negotiate wages, hours and conditions through elected union representatives → counterbalanced employer power in the Gilded Age.
p2: Absent in the Gilded Age: employers refused recognition → AFL made limited gains for skilled workers by bargaining with Mark Hanna and JP Morgan → unskilled had no protection.
p3: Without collective bargaining: wages cut without notice, 12-16 hour days common, child labour widespread → Homestead (1892) and Pullman (1894) showed what happened when workers resisted.

front: How did employers suppress unions in the Gilded Age?
p1: Private militias: companies hired armed agents like the Pinkertons to break strikes by force → Carnegie Steel used them at Homestead (1892).
p2: Blacklisting: known union organisers shared among employers, unable to find work elsewhere.
p3: Company towns: Pullman controlled housing, rents and wages and could evict strikers → employers also used sponsored newspapers and clergy to influence workers.

front: What was the Sherman Antitrust Act and how was it used against unions?
p1: Sherman Antitrust Act (1890): passed to break up monopolies deemed 'restraint of trade', e.g. Carnegie, Rockefeller → rarely used against corporations in practice.
p2: Attorney General Olney used it against the Pullman Strike (1894) → strike declared an illegal restraint of trade → injunction issued → Debs imprisoned.
p3: Irony: a law against monopolies became the main legal weapon against workers → used against unions until the Clayton Antitrust Act (1914) exempted them.

front: What was the story of the Homestead Strike (1892)?
p1: Carnegie and Henry Frick tried to break the Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers → locked out workers, sparking a mass strike.
p2: Frick hired 300 Pinkertons → battle on the Monongahela river, 12 killed, Pinkertons surrendered → Governor Pattison deployed 8,000 state militia → workers lost control of the plant.
p3: Strike collapsed November 1892, all rehired without union recognition → an anarchist tried to assassinate Frick (failed), increasing public support for Frick.

front: What was the story and significance of the Pullman Strike (1894)?
p1: Pullman cut wages 25% but not company-town rents → Debs' ARU refused to handle Pullman cars → nationwide rail paralysis → AFL refused support.
p2: Cleveland sent 12,000 troops → Olney used the Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) to win an injunction → Debs jailed 6 months.
p3: First federal injunction used to break a strike → Debs radicalised in prison, later Socialist candidate for President (6% of the vote, 1912).

front: How did the Supreme Court hinder union and labour rights in the early 20th century?
p1: Freedom of contract doctrine: courts ruled labour protections unconstitutional → Lochner v New York (1905) struck down 10-hour workday → Adkins v Children's Hospital (1923) struck down minimum wage.
p2: Coppage v Kansas (1915): upheld yellow-dog contracts, letting employers require workers to sign away union rights → stood until Norris-LaGuardia Act (1932).
p3: Duplex v Deering (1921): upheld injunctions against secondary boycotts → weakened Clayton Antitrust Act (1914) protections.

front: What was the significance of the Great Coal Strike (1902)?
p1: 140,000 miners demanded higher wages, shorter hours and union recognition → President Roosevelt arbitrated rather than send troops → first time federal government acted as mediator, not suppressor.
p2: Mitchell's moderate UMWA leadership secured presidential support → owners agreed to wage increase and improved conditions.
p3: Partial success, a shift in Progressive Era attitude → BUT no formal union recognition → showed moderate leadership could achieve more than confrontation.

front: What was the significance of the IWW and Lawrence Textile Strike?
p1: IWW ('Wobblies') founded 1905 → sought to unite all workers regardless of skill, including immigrants and minorities excluded by the AFL.
p2: Lawrence Textile 'Bread and Roses' Strike (1912): immigrant women from multiple ethnic groups, IWW-led → 15% pay rise and overtime pay.
p3: Showed the power of solidarity across ethnic lines → BUT IWW's radical tactics led to its suppression.

front: What was the significance of the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire (1911)?
p1: Triangle Shirtwaist Factory, New York, March 1911 → fire broke out → owners had locked exit doors → 146 garment workers killed, mostly young Italian and Jewish immigrant women.
p2: 100,000 marched at victims' funeral → New York Factory Commission led by Frances Perkins → 36 new labour laws enacted.
p3: Perkins later used findings to shape New Deal legislation → showed male union neglect had lethal consequences → WTUL used tragedy to build pressure for state-level reform.

front: How significant was legislation of the Progressive Era for union and labour rights?
p1: Clayton Antitrust Act (1914), 'labour's Magna Carta': exempted unions from antitrust law, banned injunctions against peaceful strikes → gutted by Duplex v Deering (1921) within 7 years.
p2: Keating-Owen Child Labour Act (1916): first federal ban on interstate sale of goods made with child labour → struck down by Hammer v Dagenhart (1918).
p3: Department of Labour (1913): first Cabinet department for workers' interests → survived intact.

front: What was the significance of the Women's Trade Union League (1903)?
p1: Coalition of working-class women and middle-class reformers → advocated better wages, shorter hours and unionisation for women workers.
p2: Exposed the exclusion of women from male-dominated unions like the AFL.
p3: Limits: AFL remained hostile to women's full membership → Triangle Shirtwaist Fire (1911) exposed inadequate protections.

front: What was the impact of WWI and the Red Scare on labour?
p1: NWLB (1918): Wilson agreement with AFL to maintain wartime production → unions accepted no-strike pledges → AFL membership grew from 2m to 3.2m.
p2: NWLB dissolved at war's end → pent-up wartime grievances erupted into a post-war strike wave, most notably the Seattle General Strike (1919).
p3: Red Scare: Bolshevik Revolution fuelled fear of communist revolution → Seattle strike branded a Bolshevist plot and crushed → unions linked to communism, weakening the AFL.

front: What was the significance of the Seattle General Strike (1919)?
p1: 65,000 workers across industries struck in solidarity → largest general strike in US history to that point → showed cross-industry solidarity beyond a single workplace.
p2: Mayor Ole Hanson denounced it as a Bolshevist revolution → press branded strikers anarchists and communists → strike collapsed without gains.
p3: Red Scare (1919): Bolshevik Revolution fuelled fears of communist revolution → union activity viewed with suspicion → post-WWI labour gains rapidly reversed.

front: What was the impact of welfare capitalism in the 1920s?
p1: Employers offered pensions, healthcare and benefits → reduced the need for unions → Ford paid $6 a day, extending his 1914 high-wage strategy.
p2: Yellow-dog contracts widespread → workers signed away the right to join unions → Philip Randolph founded the BSCP (1925) but Pullman refused recognition until 1937.
p3: Union membership fell from a 1920 peak of 5 million → Deering v Duplex (1921) restricted secondary boycotts.

front: What was the impact of the Great Depression on labour rights?
p1: Wall Street Crash (1929) → bank failures and industrial collapse → unemployment reached 25% → workers' bargaining position collapsed.
p2: Norris-LaGuardia Act (1932): barred federal injunctions against peaceful strikes and banned yellow-dog contracts → first significant legislative gain in decades.
p3: Depression showed welfare capitalism had failed → desperation drove Flint sit-down strikes and pressure for the Wagner Act.

front: What was the significance of the Wagner Act (1935)?
p1: Guaranteed the right to unionise and bargain collectively → NLRB established to enforce → banned company spies, company unions, blacklisting and dismissal of organisers.
p2: Wagner Act promoted closed shops → this inadvertently excluded Black workers from AFL unions → Social Security (1935) also excluded farm and domestic workers.
p3: First time federal government legally recognised the right to organise → BUT relied on Southern Democrats, who used local administration to undermine it.

front: What was the significance of the CIO and Flint Sit-Down Strike?
p1: John Lewis formed the CIO (1935) as part of the AFL → organised industrial workers regardless of skill, including women and African Americans.
p2: Flint Sit-Down Strike (1936-37): CIO workers at General Motors occupied the factory rather than picketing → harder to replace → UAW recognised after 44 days.
p3: Turning point for industrial unions → inspired 200 further sit-down strikes → US Steel unionised 1937 without a strike → NLRB v Fansteel (1939) ruled sit-down strikes illegal.

front: What was the significance of Philip Randolph and the BSCP?
p1: BSCP founded 1925 → first successful Black union → Randolph first African American to lead a national union winning a collective bargaining agreement (1937).
p2: March on Washington Movement (1941): threatened 100,000-strong march → Roosevelt issued EO 8802 banning discrimination in defence industries.
p3: BSCP's success relied on the New Deal shift in federal attitudes → Randolph's non-violent mass pressure became a model for the civil rights movement.

front: What was the significance of the Fair Labor Standards Act (1938)?
p1: FLSA (1938): $25 weekly minimum wage, the first federal minimum wage → maximum working hours legislated → Child labour under 16 banned in interstate commerce.
p2: Passed despite opposition from business groups → showed the New Deal coalition could overcome employer resistance.
p3: Limits: did not address the gender pay gap → excluded farm and domestic workers, sectors with many Black and immigrant workers.

front: What was the NIRA/NRA (1933) and why did it fail?
p1: NIRA (1933): codes set minimum wages, maximum hours and child labour bans → Section 7a gave workers the right to organise → Blue Eagle marked compliant firms.
p2: Declared unconstitutional in Schechter Poultry v US (1935) → exceeded federal power → many employers had displayed the Blue Eagle while ignoring codes.
p3: NIRA's voluntary codes proved insufficient → failure led directly to the Wagner Act (1935) with real NLRB enforcement.

front: What was employer and state resistance to New Deal labour reforms?
p1: Employers kept blacklisting and spy networks despite the NLRB → Ford's thugs beat UAW organisers in the Battle of the Overpass (1937).
p2: Memorial Day Massacre (1937): Chicago police killed 10 striking steelworkers at Republic Steel → local and state police acted as private armies.
p3: BUT resistance eventually failed: US Steel unionised 1937 → Ford recognised the UAW in 1941 → membership rose from 3 million (1933) to 9 million (1938).

front: What was the impact of McCarthyism on the labour movement?
p1: Taft-Hartley (1947) required union leaders to sign anti-communist oaths → those who refused lost NLRB access → McCarthyism (1947-57) intensified suspicion of unions.
p2: CIO expelled 11 radical unions (1949-50), those most inclusive of Black workers and women → AFL-CIO merger (1955) under moderate leadership.
p3: FBI COINTELPRO targeted radical organisers, with figures such as Du Bois surveilled → labour-left alliance fractured → membership peaked at 35% (1945) then declined.

front: What was the experience of workers during WWII?
p1: NWLB (1942) mediated wartime disputes → unions accepted no-strike pledges in exchange for recognition.
p2: Smith-Connally Act (1943): government could seize strike-threatened industries, passed over FDR's veto → membership soared to 14.8 million (35% of workforce) by 1945.
p3: Limits: NWLB mainly benefited AFL affiliates → pent-up frustration erupted in 5,000 strikes in 1946.

front: What was the post-WWII strike wave and how did it lead to Taft-Hartley?
p1: 1946: 5,000 strikes involving 4.6 million workers → largest strike wave in US history → steel, auto, coal and railways struck at once after wartime no-strike pledges.
p2: Taft-Hartley (1947) passed over Truman's veto → banned secondary strikes and closed shops → 60-day cooling-off period for strikes threatening national security → allowed right-to-work laws.
p3: Anti-communist oaths weakened the CIO → leaders who refused lost NLRB access → McCarthyism compounded this → rollback from 35% membership peak.

front: What was the right to exist and collectively bargain in the 1950s–60s?
p1: AFL and CIO merged in 1955 → 16 million members, 85% of the unionised workforce → members earned 20% more than non-union workers.
p2: Kennedy's EO 10988 (1962): federal employees gained the right to organise, not strike → first extension of collective bargaining to the public sector.
p3: BUT automation undercut it → manufacturing jobs declined 1950s-70s → blue-collar unions weakened → manufacturing employment down 40% from 1970 peak by 1979.

front: What was the significance of Cesar Chavez and the UFW?
p1: United Farm Workers (1966): Chavez organised Filipino and Mexican American farm workers, historically without union representation and excluded from most labour legislation.
p2: Tactics: nonviolent strikes, consumer boycotts and hunger strikes modelled on Gandhi → Delano Grape Strike (1965-70) built public support → fasting drew Robert Kennedy's support.
p3: Salad Bowl Strike (1970): Filipino-led, backed by Mexican and other workers → better wages and union recognition → California Agricultural Labor Relations Act (1975) protected farm workers' bargaining rights.

front: What was the impact of automation and deindustrialisation?
p1: Automation (1950s-70s) displaced skilled workers → blue-collar manufacturing unions weakened → membership fell as industry contracted.
p2: Deindustrialisation: steel, auto and textiles moved South or overseas → Rust Belt cities (Detroit, Pittsburgh, Cleveland) hit hardest → union strongholds collapsed.
p3: Unions negotiated severance pay and retraining → limited success → PATCO (1981) showed vulnerability, as Reagan used automation as an argument to deny reinstatement.

front: What labour legislation came out of the Kennedy and LBJ administrations?
p1: Kennedy's Equal Pay Act (1963): first federal law banning pay discrimination by sex → women earned 59¢ per $1, rising to 71¢ by 1973, though enforcement stayed limited.
p2: LBJ's Civil Rights Act (1964) Title VII banned employment discrimination by race, colour, religion, sex and national origin → EEOC enforced it → NOW (1966) formed partly to pressure the EEOC.
p3: Great Society: Medicare/Medicaid (1965) and Age Discrimination Act (1968) → BUT glass ceiling persisted for women and Black workers in management.

front: What was the significance of OSHA (1970)?
p1: OSHA (1970): first comprehensive federal workplace safety law → set minimum safety standards across industries → required employers to report injuries and deaths.
p2: Impact: workplace fatalities fell from over 14,000 annually in the 1930s to approximately 4,500 by the 1990s.
p3: Limits: Reagan cut OSHA funding → violations persisted in agriculture and construction → agricultural workers excluded from key provisions.

front: What was the significance of DRUM and the LRBW?
p1: DRUM (Dodge Revolutionary Union Movement, 1968): formed in Detroit → organised wildcat strikes in Dodge plants → demanded racial equality for Black workers in the UAW.
p2: LRBW: umbrella organisation pushing for Black leadership in the UAW → Black workers about 30% of members by the early 1970s but underrepresented in leadership → earned $2,000 less annually.
p3: UAW leadership resisted, despite similar tactics having founded the CIO → LRBW collapsed by the mid-1970s through internal divisions and FBI COINTELPRO surveillance.

front: What was the impact of the PATCO Strike (1981)?
p1: Air traffic controllers struck for a $10,000 pay rise and better conditions → Reagan declared the strike illegal → fired 11,000 and banned them from federal employment → union decertified.
p2: Shifted the balance of power → emboldened employers to adopt anti-union stances → union-busting, outsourcing and temporary workers became normal.
p3: PATCO alienated the public, striking over summer holidays → made Reagan's response politically easy → union membership already down to 24% (1979).

front: What was the impact of Reaganomics on labour rights?
p1: Deregulation and tax cuts for business → union-busting became standard practice → employers used legal challenges, outsourcing and temporary workers to weaken unions.
p2: Reagan cut OSHA funding → safety violations persisted in agriculture and construction → employer-friendly judicial appointments weakened NLRB enforcement.
p3: By 1992 union membership had dropped to 16% of the workforce, from 24% in 1979 → showed the longer trajectory PATCO helped set in motion.

front: What was the right to exist and collectively bargain by 1992?
p1: Wagner Act (1935) legally protected collective bargaining → NLRB enforced it → BUT Taft-Hartley (1947) allowed right-to-work laws in 21 states.
p2: PATCO (1981): Reagan fired 11,000 controllers → emboldened employers → union-busting consultants and outsourcing became standard.
p3: Membership collapsed from 35% (1945) to 16% (1992) → AFL-CIO members still earned 20% more → bargaining legally protected but practically weakened.

front: What was the right to strike by 1992?
p1: Right to strike legally protected but restricted → Taft-Hartley banned secondary strikes and closed shops → Norris-LaGuardia (1932) had removed injunctions, but Taft-Hartley reintroduced restrictions.
p2: PATCO (1981) showed strikes could be broken with mass dismissals → major strikes fell from 381 (1970) to under 40 (1992).
p3: Right-to-work laws in 21 states undermined solidarity → outsourcing and automation reduced leverage → strike weapon largely neutered by 1992.

front: What were fair and safe working conditions by 1992?
p1: OSHA (1970): workplace deaths fell from 14,000+ to 4,500 annually → FLSA set minimum wage, maximum hours and a child labour ban → Equal Pay Act (1963) and Title VII (1964) banned pay discrimination.
p2: BUT Reagan cut OSHA funding → violations persisted in agriculture and construction → agricultural workers still excluded from key FLSA provisions.
p3: Glass ceiling persisted → Black workers still earned $2,000 less than white equivalents → enforcement of equal pay legislation remained weak.

front: What was Manifest Destiny and its impact on Native Americans?
p1: Manifest Destiny: white American settlement of the continent from coast to coast was divinely ordained → moral and religious justification for Native displacement.
p2: Social Darwinism framed Native Americans as 'backward' on an inferior rung of civilisation → eugenic theories seen as modern science → racial separation and cultural destruction justified as progress.
p3: Underpinned the Plains Wars, Dawes Act and boarding schools → settlers fulfilling a divine purpose → IRA (1882): white missionaries saw assimilation as a Christian duty.

front: What was the reservation system and how did it work?
p1: Federal policy confining Native tribes to designated land areas, managed by the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) → began with the Indian Removal Act (1830s), systematised after the Plains Wars.
p2: BIA took increasing control, corrupt and paternalistic → reservations on poor, infertile land → Natives dependent on insufficient government rations → tuberculosis 25% above national average.
p3: By 1900 only 100,000 of 240,000 Plains Indians remained → Dawes Act (1887) broke up even reservation land → 'ghettos in the wilderness', dependency replacing self-sufficiency.

front: What was the right to land for Native Americans in 1865?
p1: Indian Removal Act (1830s) legacy: southeastern tribes already in Indian Territory (Oklahoma) → Plains tribes like the Sioux held vast territories but under pressure from westward expansion.
p2: Homestead Act (1862): 160-acre plots to settlers encroached on Native lands → Fort Laramie Treaty (1868) recognised land rights but confined tribes.
p3: Transcontinental railroad (1869) opened the West to settlers → Natives excluded from Homestead Act opportunities → no citizenship, 'wards of the state'.

front: What was the right to self-determination for Native Americans in 1865?
p1: Tribes legally recognised as sovereign nations → able to make treaties with the federal government → own governance systems, with tribal chiefs holding authority.
p2: BUT Indian Appropriations Act (1871) would end treaty-making → tribes no longer independent nations → BIA managed Native affairs paternalistically and corruptly.
p3: Plains Wars (1854-77) ongoing, with troops and militias used systematically → Manifest Destiny: white settlement divinely ordained → self-determination about to be dismantled.

front: What were cultural and religious freedoms for Native Americans in 1865?
p1: Cultures, languages and governance largely intact → buffalo central to spiritual and cultural life → ceremonies continued freely on still-controlled territories.
p2: BUT Christian missionaries already on reservations → assimilation promoted as a 'civilising' mission → Carlisle boarding school (1879) coming: 'kill the Indian, save the man'.
p3: Ghost Dance suppression (1890) still 25 years away → no federal ban on ceremonies yet → cultural destruction planned but not fully implemented.

front: What were the broader political and economic rights of Native Americans in 1865?
p1: No citizenship → no vote → no standing in federal courts or representation in Congress → BIA managed all relations, acting as both administrator and judge.
p2: Economy: buffalo-based subsistence, entirely self-sufficient → communal land ownership → no dependence on federal rations → BUT Homestead Act (1862) already threatening this base.
p3: No tax obligations as non-citizens → BUT no access to federal economic programmes → no wage labour except on settlers' terms → independence about to be destroyed.

front: What was the impact of treaty-making with Native Americans?
p1: Before 1871, Native tribes treated as foreign states → treaties agreed land and created reservations, usually after conflict → often signed under alcohol, with poor translation or without the chief.
p2: First Treaty of Fort Laramie (1851) created the Great Sioux Reservation → violated by settlers and prospectors → Red Cloud's War (1866-68) a Native victory → Second Treaty (1868) granted Black Hills to the Sioux forever.
p3: Second Treaty also violated after Custer found gold in the Black Hills in 1874.

front: What was the impact of the Civil War and Plains Wars on Natives?
p1: Civil War (1861-65) consumed the regular US Army → frontier defence left to volunteer militias, less disciplined and more prone to atrocity.
p2: Sand Creek Massacre (1864): militia killed 150+ Cheyenne while federal attention was on the Confederacy → Plains Wars (1854-77) escalated → tribes allied with the Confederacy weakened post-war.
p3: Scale: 70+ Native tribes forcibly relocated to reservations by the end of the Plains Wars → freedom of movement and land access severely curtailed.

front: What was the significance of the Battle of Little Bighorn (1876)?
p1: Crazy Horse and Sitting Bull led 2,000+ Sioux warriors → annihilated Custer's 7th Cavalry (268 dead) → largest Native military victory of the Plains Wars.
p2: Army flooded the Plains with reinforcements → Sitting Bull fled to Canada → Crazy Horse surrendered and was killed in custody (1877) → Black Hills seized in violation of Fort Laramie Treaty.
p3: Briefly raised morale but accelerated federal military response → proved Natives could win battles, not the war → by 1877 major armed resistance effectively ended.

front: What was the impact of the Homestead Act and railroad on Natives?
p1: Homestead Act (1862): settlers granted 160-acre plots on Native lands → 270 million acres distributed by 1900 → tribes displaced from ancestral territories.
p2: Transcontinental railroad (1869) opened the Plains to mass settlement → destroyed buffalo migration routes → buffalo fell from 30 million (1800) to under 1,000 (1889); Army killed 10 million 1865-83.
p3: Plains tribes lost economic base and territorial integrity within a decade → forced onto marginal reservation land → set conditions for Dawes Act dispossession.

front: What was the Long Walk of the Navajo (1864–66)?
p1: Kit Carson destroyed Navajo crops, orchards and livestock to force surrender → 8,000-9,000 Navajo marched 300 miles to Bosque Redondo in winter → thousands died.
p2: Bosque Redondo: barren, alkaline soil and contaminated water → crops failed repeatedly → 3,000 Navajo died in four years → rationing inadequate, BIA agents corrupt.
p3: Treaty of 1868: Navajo allowed to return to ancestral lands, one of the few treaty victories of the period → reservation expanded 4 million acres.

front: What was the Indian Appropriations Act (1871)?
p1: Indian Appropriations Act (1871): tribes no longer independent nations → ended treaty-making → tribes became 'wards of state' with no legal standing to challenge dispossession.
p2: BIA agents took increasing control of reservation life → allotment of individual plots replaced communal land → tribes lost the ability to govern themselves.
p3: Transformed the legal relationship between tribes and federal government → enabled the Dawes Act (1887) and dispossession without treaty obligations.

front: What was the Dawes Severalty Act (1887) and how did it work?
p1: Dawes Severalty Act (1887): divided communal tribal land into 160-acre allotments → 'surplus' sold to white settlers → Curtis Act (1898) extended it to the Five Civilised Tribes.
p2: Native-owned land fell from 156 million acres (1887) to 78 million by 1900 → most allotments lost through sale, fraud or inheritance division.
p3: Allottees lacked farming experience or capital → many sold to survive → undermined the policy's stated goal of creating self-sufficient farmers.

front: What was the cultural impact of the Dawes Act?
p1: Imposed male-headed family ownership on matriarchal tribes → Iroquois and Cherokee women traditionally managed land → Dawes Act stripped this role.
p2: Allotment scattered families across individual plots → broke up tribal concentration → undermined communal ceremonies, governance and economic co-operation.
p3: A few Native Americans prospered as individual landowners, but this was the rare exception for the vast majority who lost their land.

front: What were the key court cases and laws that destroyed Native sovereignty after 1883?
p1: Crow Dog Case (1883): tribal criminal jurisdiction recognised → BUT Congress responded with the Major Crimes Act (1885): federal jurisdiction over 7 serious crimes on reservations.
p2: Cherokee Nation v Hitchcock (1902): Congress had plenary authority over Native affairs → Lone Wolf v Hitchcock (1903): Congress could unilaterally revoke treaties.
p3: Dead Indian Act (1902) allowed sale of inherited allotment land → accelerated dispossession → together these closed all legal avenues for Native resistance.

front: What was the Ghost Dance Movement (1889) and what did it represent?
p1: Founded by Wovoka (Paiute prophet) in 1889 → 5 days of dancing blended traditional beliefs with Christian hope of a messiah restoring Native lands and buffalo.
p2: Government alarmed by mass gatherings, seen as a military threat → Sitting Bull arrested and killed → 7th Cavalry surrounded Lakota at Wounded Knee (1890): 250 men, women and children killed.
p3: End of armed Plains Indian resistance → Ghost Dance suppressed, the last major cultural resistance movement of the period → Wounded Knee became an enduring symbol of Native suffering.

front: What was the boarding school system in the Gilded Age?
p1: Carlisle Indian Industrial School (Pennsylvania, 1879): Colonel Richard Pratt, 'kill the Indian, save the man' → model for federal boarding schools → children forbidden languages, traditions and traditional clothing.
p2: 100,000+ children forced into boarding schools by the early 1900s → death rates 30-50% from neglect, abuse and malnutrition.
p3: Graduates returned alienated from both worlds → trauma passed through generations → contributed to high alcoholism and suicide rates on reservations.

front: What was the role of Helen Hunt Jackson and the Indian Rights Association?
p1: A Century of Dishonour (1881): Helen Hunt Jackson documented broken treaties and massacres → sent to every member of Congress → influenced reform debates.
p2: Indian Rights Association (IRA, 1882): white reformers advocated Native education and citizenship → pushed the Dawes Act as a path to 'civilisation' → imposed white assimilationist values.
p3: Limits: raised awareness but led to the Dawes Act, which caused further land loss → reformers prioritised assimilation over sovereignty.

front: What was the impact of reservations on Native Americans? (positives)
p1: Reservations let tribal life continue in limited forms → cultural identity and community sustained → better healthcare than a nomadic lifestyle, though limited → some gained jobs as interpreters, scouts or Indian Agency workers.
p2: Navajo success: reservation expanded from 4 million to 10.5 million acres → Sheep and goats 15,000 to 1.7 million → population 8,000 (1868) to 22,000 by 1900, the only major demographic recovery.
p3: Reservations gave defined land holdings that could be defended legally → basis for later sovereignty arguments, though limited by BIA paternalism.

front: What was the impact of reservations on Native Americans? (limitations)
p1: Land infertile and hard to farm → many dependent on insufficient government rations, often cut or mismanaged → by 1900 only 100,000 of 240,000 Plains Indians remained.
p2: BIA corrupt: agents stole rations and manipulated accounts → 1871 Act abolished tribal sovereignty → no legal recourse → 'ghettos in the wilderness'.
p3: Confinement cut Native Americans off from hunting grounds, sacred sites and land-based practices, disrupting their spiritual connection with the environment.

front: What were the damaging effects of assimilation policies in the Gilded Age?
p1: Dawes Act: Native-owned land fell from 156 million acres (1881) to 78 million by 1900 → allotments often poor quality → most sold or lost within a generation.
p2: Cultural suppression beyond schooling: Sun Dance banned, buffalo hunting forbidden → spiritual and subsistence practices outlawed outright.
p3: Land given to male heads of families → matriarchal structures weakened → dependency on government rations replaced self-sufficiency.

front: What was the role of the Five Civilised Tribes and Sequoyah Convention?
p1: Five Civilised Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, Seminole): written constitutions, elected governments, mixed economy → occupied Indian Territory → exempt from Dawes allotment until the Curtis Act (1898).
p2: Curtis Act (1898): destroyed their governments, allotment imposed without consent → Sequoyah Convention (1905): leaders proposed an all-Native state → democratic response to dispossession.
p3: Congress rejected Sequoyah → Oklahoma created 1907, merging Indian Territory with Oklahoma Territory → showed Native Americans could govern successfully on their own terms.

front: What was the role of BIA corruption and paternalism?
p1: Tribes became 'wards of state' after the Indian Appropriations Act (1871) → no legal standing → BIA agents controlled access to schools, healthcare, employment and housing.
p2: Corruption: agents took commissions from contractors and misallocated rations → late 1880s: meat subsidies to Sioux reservations cut as disease devastated cattle herds → starvation.
p3: Paternalism: BIA assumed Native Americans incapable of self-governance → decisions made without tribal consultation → dependency reinforced, conditions deteriorated.

front: What was the significance of the Society of American Indians (SAI, 1911)?
p1: Society of American Indians (SAI, 1911): first national Native American rights organisation led by educated Native Americans → advocated citizenship, land reform and the end of the BIA.
p2: Carlos Montezuma demanded abolition of the BIA → Gertrude Bonnin (Zitkala-Sa) documented boarding school trauma → Arthur Parker promoted Native history and pride.
p3: Limits: divided between assimilationists and sovereignty supporters, split over peyote use → collapsed by the 1920s → established the pan-tribal advocacy model.

front: What was the impact of WWI service on Native Americans?
p1: 12,000 Native Americans served in WWI (some estimates 17,000) → many not yet citizens → showed loyalty to a nation that denied them rights → used as scouts and code communicators.
p2: Wartime service directly contributed to the Indian Citizenship Act (1924), which finally granted citizenship to all Native Americans.
p3: 400 Native American soldiers awarded the Medal of Honor → raised their status in American society → BUT recognition did not translate into improved rights at home.

front: What was the significance of the Indian Citizenship Act (1924)?
p1: Citizenship granted to all Native Americans (1924) → BUT two-thirds were already citizens through Dawes Act allotments, military service or individual treaties.
p2: Many states barred Native voting through literacy tests and poll taxes → Arizona did not recognise Native voting rights until forced by courts in the late 1940s.
p3: Formal recognition as full citizens → BUT BIA retained paternalistic control → citizenship did not bring political power or economic improvement.

front: How did reformers' attitudes towards Native Americans change in the 1920s?
p1: John Collier lived among Pueblo communities in New Mexico in the 1920s → came to believe Native cultures should be preserved, not erased → founded AIDA (1923).
p2: AIDA blocked the Leavitt Bill (1926), which sought to ban traditional Pueblo dances → a cultural preservation victory and a sign reformers were shifting from assimilation to protection.
p3: Meriam Report (1928) exposed the failures of the Dawes Act era (poverty, disease, death rates) → turned federal opinion decisively against assimilation.

front: What did the Indian Reorganization Act (Wheeler-Howard Act, 1934) do?
p1: Wheeler-Howard Act (1934) halted Dawes Act allotment → recovered unallocated land, restoring 4 million of 90 million acres lost → established tribal constitutions and elected tribal councils.
p2: Established tribal corporations to manage resources → direct funding for farming, healthcare and infrastructure to tribal governments.
p3: Decisive ideological shift from assimilation to self-determination, reversing 50 years of policy → BUT 82% of Native Americans still below the poverty line by 1940.

front: What were the limitations of the Indian Reorganization Act (1934)?
p1: Collier ignored Native diversity → imposed secret-ballot constitutions on tribes used to open council discussion → of 252 tribes that voted, 174 accepted, but only 92 adopted formal constitutions.
p2: Navajo rejected the Act over livestock reduction (1933-36) → 150,000 sheep, goats and horses killed → sheep were women's property in a matrilineal society → economic and cultural devastation.
p3: Chronic underfunding: 82% below poverty line by 1940 → only $2m annually for land buyback → Navajo students got 13¢/day for lunch vs the recommended 50¢ → paternalism continued.

front: What was the role of the IECW and CCC-ID in the New Deal?
p1: Indian Emergency Conservation Work (IECW) and Civilian Conservation Corps-Indian Division (CCC-ID) gave Native Americans New Deal employment.
p2: 85,000 employed 1933-42 → planted 25 million trees, built 6,500 miles of road → surplus army clothing distributed.
p3: Indian Arts and Crafts Board (1935) revived Native arts as economic ventures → cultural education funding up 65% (1935-40) → tribal councils reinstated → ceremonial dance bans overturned.

front: What was the role of the NCAI and Indian Claims Commission?
p1: NCAI (1944): first large-scale pan-tribal advocacy organisation → opposed the federal termination policy → lobbied Congress for treaty rights.
p2: Indian Claims Commission (1946): compensated for land taken with cash, not land → $1.3 billion in claims filed by the 1950s → slow process, many denied.
p3: Limits: NCAI relied on legal channels, too slow and moderate for immediate poverty → ICC gave money not land → termination proceeded despite NCAI opposition.

front: What was the significance of Native American service in WWII?
p1: Over 25,000 Native Americans served in WWII → fought for democracy abroad while denied rights at home → Japanese American internment camps built on Native land.
p2: Navajo Code Talkers: 400-500 marines used the Navajo language as an unbreakable code → Major Howard Connor: "Were it not for the Navajos, the Marines would never have taken Iwo Jima".
p3: Service did not bring equality: veterans returned to poverty and BIA control → GI Bill benefits (education, housing loans) hard to access on reservations.

front: What was the Termination Policy (1953) and what were its consequences?
p1: Termination Policy (1953-68): ended federal recognition for 109 tribes → sold their lands, ended healthcare, education and legal protections → Menominee (Wisconsin) and Klamath (Oregon) worst affected.
p2: Extreme poverty → terminated tribes lost all federal support → many lost land to private developers → Menominee hospital closed → malnutrition soared.
p3: NCAI lobbied against termination → Nixon formally ended it (1970) → Menominee Restoration Act (1973) first restored a tribe → showed termination had been a catastrophic failure.

front: What was the Indian Relocation Act (1956) and what were its consequences?
p1: Indian Relocation Act (1956): BIA gave one-way bus tickets to cities such as Chicago, Los Angeles and Denver → promised jobs and housing → by 1970, 40% of Native Americans lived in cities.
p2: Reality: urban poverty often replaced reservation poverty → substandard housing, scarce jobs → cultural isolation with no tribal community or BIA follow-up.
p3: AIM (1968) was founded in Minneapolis by urban Natives who had experienced relocation → direct line from the Relocation Act to AIM militancy.

front: What was the significance of the NIYC (1961) and the fish-ins?
p1: NIYC (1961): first militant pan-tribal youth organisation → fish-ins in the Pacific Northwest asserted treaty fishing rights, modelled on Black civil rights sit-ins.
p2: Natives exercised treaty rights in defiance of state fishing laws → arrested → national media coverage → showed treaty rights could be asserted through civil disobedience.
p3: Shift from NCAI's moderate legal approach to direct action → influenced AIM's later tactics.

front: What was life like on the reservations in the mid-20th century?
p1: 1960s: per capita income on reservations half the national average → unemployment 40-80% on many reservations → infant mortality three times the national average.
p2: BIA dependence: tribes had little control over their resources → federal funding inadequate and subject to political winds → termination (1953) devastated weak tribal economies.
p3: Urban relocation offered one route out → BUT moving to cities did not solve reservation poverty, as those who left received little ongoing support.

front: What was Red Power and how did it differ from earlier activism?
p1: Red Power: militant movement for Native rights from the late 1960s, inspired by Black Power → rejected assimilation → demanded treaty rights and sovereignty.
p2: AIM (1968): founded in Minneapolis by urban Natives, patrolling police to document brutality → Alcatraz occupation (1969-71): 'Indians of All Tribes' held it 19 months demanding unused land.
p3: Different from earlier activism: NCAI used legal channels, NIYC civil disobedience → Red Power added armed confrontation (Trail of Broken Treaties 1972, Wounded Knee 1973) and media spectacle.

front: What was the significance of the Alcatraz Occupation (1969–71)?
p1: Led by Richard Oakes (Mohawk) and 'Indians of All Tribes' → occupied Alcatraz in November 1969 → claimed the 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty gave Natives the right to unused federal land.
p2: 19-month occupation → 10,000 Natives visited → massive national media coverage and public sympathy → demanded a Native university, cultural centre and museum.
