p3: Limits: Oakes' daughter died in a fall during the occupation (1970) → he left → ended 1971 without policy changes → BUT sparked the Red Power movement nationally.

front: What was the significance of the Wounded Knee Occupation (1973)?
p1: 71-day standoff at Wounded Knee, South Dakota (1973): AIM members and Oglala Lakota occupied the town.
p2: Pine Ridge: AIM backed Oglala Lakota residents against corrupt tribal chairman Dick Wilson and his 'Guardians of the Oglala Nation' (GOONs) → marshals surrounded the village → 2 AIM members killed.
p3: Brought international attention to Native rights, compared by some to Selma → exposed BIA corruption → BUT 600+ arrested, leaders tried for years → movement fragmented.

front: What was the significance of the Trail of Broken Treaties (1972)?
p1: November 1972: caravan of multiple tribes drove to Washington DC before the presidential election → demanded restoration of Native sovereignty and treaty-making rights → occupied BIA headquarters for several days.
p2: 20-point manifesto: treaty enforcement, restoration of tribal land base, abolition of BIA → Nixon administration negotiated rather than use force, as election timing made confrontation costly.
p3: Most effective pan-tribal organisation of the Red Power era → BIA occupation symbolically powerful → led directly to Wounded Knee (1973).

front: What was the significance of Nixon ending termination and the Self-Determination Act?
p1: Nixon (1970) formally ended termination, acknowledging it had been wrong → federal recognition restored to terminated tribes → Menominee restored 1973.
p2: Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act (1975): tribes could administer their own federal programmes → BIA contracts transferred to tribal control → 200+ tribes by the late 1970s.
p3: AIRFA (1978) protected traditional practices → ICWA (1978): tribes gained authority over child welfare → shift from assimilation to self-determination complete.

front: How did the Supreme Court impact Native rights in the 1970s and 1980s?
p1: Oneida v Oneida (1974): Oneida Nation could sue for land claims under federal treaties → US v Sioux (1980): Black Hills illegally seized in 1877 → $106 million awarded → Sioux refused.
p2: Fisher v Montana (1976): tribes decide on adoptions → Bryan v Itasca (1976): states cannot tax reservations → Seminole v Butterworth (1982): tribal casino sovereignty.
p3: Charrier v Bell (1986): burial sites protected, a cultural rights victory.

front: What was the right to land for Native Americans by 1992?
p1: Indian Claims Commission (1946): awarded $800 million in compensation, but only money, not land → Sioux refused $106 million for the Black Hills as 'not for sale' → fund grew to $600m+ unclaimed.
p2: NARF secured legal victories: Oneida (1974), Fisher (1976), Bryan (1976) → some land returned through settlements → BUT 30% of Native Americans still on reservations facing land loss.
p3: Gaming Act (1988): economic use of reservation land → 150 casinos generating $1 billion+ → BUT land sovereignty still limited by federal oversight and inconsistent legal protections.

front: What was the right to self-determination for Native Americans by 1992?
p1: Indian Self-Determination Act (1975): 200+ tribes administering their own federal programmes → tribal courts recognised → AIM had forced political visibility through Alcatraz (1969) and Wounded Knee (1973).
p2: Bryan v Itasca (1976): states cannot tax reservations → tribal sovereignty affirmed in court → BUT 60% of tribes still economically reliant on federal funding.
p3: All citizens since 1924 → voting in all states since Harrison v Laveen (1948) → BUT only 50% registered to vote in 1992 → voter turnout remained low → political influence marginal.

front: What were cultural and religious freedoms for Native Americans by 1992?
p1: AIRFA (1978) protected traditional practices → BUT 70% of Native religious leaders reported ongoing struggles accessing sacred sites by 1992.
p2: Indian Arts and Crafts Act (1990) prevented exploitation by non-Native sellers → Languages Act (1990): 100+ programmes → NAGPRA (1990): 10,000+ items returned.
p3: 100+ Native language programmes active, preserving languages at risk → BUT enforcement of AIRFA remained weak → sacred sites still inaccessible.

front: What were the broader political and economic rights of Native Americans by 1992?
p1: Citizens and voters in all states by 1948 → BUT only 50% registered to vote by 1992 → voter turnout remained low → political influence marginal at federal level.
p2: Economic opportunities limited → 25% of Native families still below the poverty line → 60% reliant on federal assistance.
p3: Education: less than 60% graduated high school, only 10% held college degrees → life expectancy 5-10 years below national average.

front: What was coverture?
p1: Legal doctrine: a married woman's identity was subsumed into her husband's → could not own property, sign contracts or keep wages → no legal recourse against abusive husbands → divorce deeply stigmatised.
p2: Husbands controlled all marital property and earnings → women could not run businesses, take loans or appear in court independently → no independent legal existence.
p3: Erosion: Married Women's Property Acts (state reforms from 1870s) → Equal Credit Opportunity Act (1974) gave independent credit → ERA failed (1982), so no constitutional end to coverture-based discrimination.

front: What was the impact of separate spheres rhetoric on women in the 19th century?
p1: Men → public sphere (politics, business, law); women → private sphere (home, children) → framed as different, not inferior → women cast as morally superior but unsuited to public life.
p2: Moral guardianship framing opened a narrow route into public life → church work, charity and temperance campaigning acceptable as domestic virtue extended outward, not politics.
p3: Movements outside this frame had to adapt → abolitionist and settlement-house campaigning succeeded partly by presenting as moral, not political, causes.

front: What were the political rights of women in 1865?
p1: No vote at any level → Seneca Falls (1848) demanded suffrage with minimal gains → NWSA and AWSA not yet formed (1869) → 15th Amendment (1870) would give Black men the vote but exclude women.
p2: No right to sit on juries, hold public office or stand for election → Minor v Happersett (1875) would confirm citizenship did not guarantee the vote.
p3: Some women organising: Anthony and Stanton campaigning → WCTU formed 1874 → Wyoming Territory granted female suffrage 1869.

front: What was the social position of women in 1865?
p1: Coverture: husband controlled all property, contracts and wages → average 5-7 children → 1 in 5 died in childbirth → only 3% attended college vs 25% of men.
p2: Cult of domesticity confined women to the 'private sphere' → any paid work seen as failure of the husband's duty → immigrant women worked 70 hours/week in sweatshops.
p3: Comstock Laws (1873) would criminalise contraceptive information → no reproductive rights → divorce almost impossible → domestic violence not recognised as a crime.

front: What was the economic position of women in 1865?
p1: 15% employed outside the home → 17% in industrial jobs at half male wages → 40% of Black women in the South in domestic service, with no legal protection or union membership.
p2: AFL-CIO not yet formed but predecessor unions excluded women → KOL (1869) the only major union to welcome them → 400,000+ Civil War widows with no financial safety net.
p3: No minimum wage, no maternity rights, no equal pay legislation → coverture meant women could not own property or sign contracts independently.

front: What was the significance of Susan B. Anthony?
p1: NWSA (1869): founded with Stanton → demanded a federal constitutional amendment for suffrage → broader women's rights: property, divorce, employment.
p2: Attempted to vote (1872) → arrested in Rochester, fined $100 → refused to pay → national publicity for the suffrage cause.
p3: NWSA refused to support the 15th Amendment, which gave Black men the vote but excluded women → damaged relations with abolitionists → revealed tensions within reform.

front: What was the impact of Reconstruction on women's rights?
p1: 15th Amendment (1870): vote for Black men, not women → NWSA (Anthony/Stanton) opposed it → AWSA (Stone) supported it → split weakened the suffrage movement for 20 years.
p2: Anthony's arrest for voting became a rallying point → Wyoming Territory granted female suffrage (1869) → Women's Crusade (1873): 50,000 marched → WCTU founded (1874).
p3: Black women excluded from both NWSA and AWSA → Reconstruction Congress focused on African American male rights → women's suffrage treated as a secondary question.

front: What were the Comstock Laws (1873)?
p1: Comstock Laws (1873): federal law making distribution of 'obscene' materials illegal → explicitly included contraceptives and abortion information → 4,000 arrests by 1900.
p2: Reproductive decisions criminalised → wealthy women accessed contraception through private doctors → working-class and immigrant women had none → class inequality worsened.
p3: Early challenge by Emma Goldman and others → arrested repeatedly for distributing birth control information → showed the state actively policed women's bodies.

front: What was the significance of Frances Willard and the WCTU?
p1: WCTU (1874): Frances Willard led from 1879 → 'Do Everything' strategy of temperance + suffrage + social reform → largest women's organisation in the world by the 1890s.
p2: Lobbied for the 8-hour day, prison reform and kindergartens alongside temperance → 300,000 members by the 1890s → Willard died 1898 before any amendments.
p3: Divisions: temperance imposed middle-class Protestant values → alienated Catholic immigrant and working-class women → narrow moral focus limited coalition-building.

front: What was the significance of Jane Addams and Hull House?
p1: Hull House (1889): founded in Chicago → 2,000+ people served per week by its second year → social services, education and cultural programmes for poor immigrant women and families.
p2: Addams lobbied for child labour laws, the 8-hour day and workplace safety → National Consumers League link → brought middle-class reformers into working-class communities.
p3: Linked social work to political reform → cross-class solidarity → 400 settlement houses nationwide → BUT focused on assimilation of immigrants.

front: What were working conditions like for women in the Gilded Age?
p1: Women earned about half of male wages throughout → immigrant women: 70 hours/week for $5 → domestic service paid $3-5/week with no protections → clerical workers slightly better.
p2: Factory work unventilated, unlit and dangerous → no safety regulations or workers' compensation → owners could lock exits, as Triangle Shirtwaist would later expose.
p3: AFL excluded most women → male unions opposed women working → Women's Trade Union League (WTUL, 1903) filled the gap with limited success.

front: What were the gains for women during the Gilded Age?
p1: 111,000 women in higher education (21%) by 1870 → 32% by 1880 → by 1900 half of high school graduates were female → access to teaching, secretarial and nursing professions.
p2: Wyoming (1869), Colorado (1893), Utah and Idaho (1896) granted female suffrage → 4 states by the end of the period.
p3: The birth rate fell from 5.42 (1850) to 3.56 (1900) → reduced domestic burden → by 1900 c.1 million working women as teachers, secretaries, librarians and telephone operators.

front: What were the limits on women's progress during the Gilded Age?
p1: Women paid half male wages throughout the period → immigrant women worked 70 hours/week for just $5.
p2: Education gains and reform participation alike reached the white middle class only → working-class women lacked the time, money and social access to join.
p3: Comstock Laws (1873) criminalised contraceptive information → blocked reproductive autonomy regardless of class or education.

front: How effective were women's movements in the Gilded Age?
p1: NWSA's militant tactics generated national publicity → AWSA's state-by-state campaigning won real victories where NWSA's federal push could not.
p2: Women's Crusade (1873) built the momentum that founded the WCTU (1874), a mass social campaign reaching women nationwide.
p3: Jane Addams founded Hull House (1889), offering social services to immigrant women in Chicago → YWCA (1867) did similar practical work for urban women.

front: How ineffective were women's movements in the Gilded Age?
p1: Male unions refused to back women's strikes (1882 Lawrence textile workers got no union support) → only 2% of trade unionists were women by 1900 → AFL excluded women outright.
p2: Minor v Happersett (1875) confirmed citizenship did not guarantee the vote → blocked the constitutional route to suffrage entirely.
p3: No federal suffrage secured despite over 30 years of campaigning → moral persuasion alone could not convert into political power.

front: How united were women in the Gilded Age?
p1: NWSA and AWSA, despite tactical differences, both pushed for suffrage → merged into NAWSA (1890), laying the foundation for the 19th Amendment.
p2: WCTU united women across class lines around a shared cause (temperance) → largest women's organisation in the world.
p3: By 1900 half of all high school graduates were female and c.1 million women worked outside the home → shared experience that helped narrow the middle-class and working-class gap.

front: How divided were women in the Gilded Age?
p1: Middle-class women focused on suffrage and temperance → working-class immigrant women on wages and survival (70 hours/week in sweatshops) → resented temperance as cultural interference.
p2: Black women excluded from NAWSA → Ida B. Wells excluded from the 1913 suffrage march → National Association of Colored Women (1896) formed as a separate, necessary organisation.
p3: NWSA and AWSA split energy and resources between strategies → Anti-Suffrage League organised to block the vote, arguing women's place was in the home.

front: What was the significance of Carrie Chapman Catt and NAWSA?
p1: NAWSA (1890): merger of NWSA and AWSA under Catt → 'Winning Plan' (1916) combined state campaigns with a federal amendment push → 2 million members by 1919.
p2: 19th Amendment (1920): NAWSA's 50-year campaign succeeded → Catt founded the League of Women Voters immediately after, to educate the new electorate.
p3: Limits: NAWSA prioritised white Southern women's support → Black women forced to march at the back of the 1913 Suffrage Parade.

front: What was the significance of Alice Paul?
p1: CUWS (1913): Paul and Lucy Burns used militant tactics, picketing the White House → 7-month prison sentence, hunger strikes → force-fed → massive publicity.
p2: Silent Sentinels: daily White House pickets from 1917 with 'Kaiser Wilson' banners → arrested 168 times → publicity forced Wilson to reverse opposition to suffrage.
p3: ERA (1923): Paul first introduced the Equal Rights Amendment, demanding immediate legal equality → opposed by social feminists who feared losing protective labour legislation.

front: What was the significance of the Triangle Shirtwaist Fire (1911)?
p1: New York City, March 1911 → fire on the upper floors of the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory → owners had locked exit doors.
p2: 100,000 marched at the victims' funeral → New York Factory Commission, a comprehensive investigation led by Frances Perkins.
p3: Galvanised the labour movement around women workers' safety → Perkins later used the findings to shape the New Deal → showed male union neglect had lethal consequences.

front: What was the significance of the Bread and Roses Strike (1912)?
p1: Lawrence, Massachusetts: mill owners cut wages after a 54-hour week law reduced hours → 20,000+ immigrant women struck, IWW-led → 51 nationalities.
p2: Tactics: picketing, marches, children sent to union families in other cities → public sympathy → no male union support → Elizabeth Gurley Flynn central to leadership.
p3: Success: 15% pay rise, overtime pay, no discrimination against strikers → showed immigrant working-class women could win through solidarity.

front: What was the impact of WWI on women's rights?
p1: 40% of women employed during the war → entered manufacturing, engineering and transport → proved women could do traditionally male roles → but mostly replaced by returning soldiers.
p2: WWI service strengthened the suffrage argument ('if you fight, you vote') → Wilson reversed his opposition → 19th Amendment passed 1919, ratified 1920.
p3: Limited gains: most women returned to domestic roles → wages dropped → trade unions excluded women → wartime opportunity was temporary, not transformative.

front: What was the impact of the 19th Amendment (1920)?
p1: 19th Amendment (1920): vote granted after 50 years → BUT only 1/3 of women voted vs 2/3 of men in the 1920s → low political engagement in the first decade.
p2: Black women faced voter suppression in the South through poll taxes, literacy tests and violence → 19th Amendment theoretical for them until the Voting Rights Act.
p3: Women slow to enter political office → Nellie Tayloe Ross (first female governor, 1925) → League of Women Voters educated but did not transform participation.

front: What was the significance of Margaret Sanger?
p1: Brooklyn clinic (1916): served 20,000 women → shut down for violating Comstock Laws → Sanger arrested and jailed → continued campaign from exile.
p2: American Birth Control League (ABCL, 1921): increased access to contraception → lobbied Congress to exempt birth control from obscenity laws → 222 clinics by the 1930s.
p3: Shepherd-Towner Act (1921): first federal maternity and infant health funding, ABCL lobbied alongside → BUT funding ended 1929 and Comstock Laws remained → eugenics controversy undermined Sanger's legacy.

front: What was flapper culture and what did it represent?
p1: Young, urban, white, middle-class women: dancing, smoking, drinking, short hair and skirts → challenged Victorian femininity → birth rate falling, marriage age rising.
p2: BUT limited to the white urban middle class → rural, working-class, Black and immigrant women unaffected or hostile.
p3: Real cultural change, but widespread opposition to women working, especially once married, limited how far it went → Comstock Laws still in force.

front: What was the impact of leading political women in the New Deal?
p1: Frances Perkins: first female Cabinet member, Secretary of Labour 1933-45 → shaped FLSA (1938) and the Social Security Act (1935).
p2: Eleanor Roosevelt transformed the First Lady role: press conferences, newspaper column, pushed FDR on appointments → resigned from the DAR to support Marian Anderson (1939).
p3: Florence Allen: first female Circuit Court judge → Mary McLeod Bethune led the NYA's Division of Negro Affairs → wider circle of women gained institutional power under FDR.

front: What were the limitations of the New Deal for women?
p1: FLSA (1938) set a minimum wage but reinforced the gender pay gap → CCC excluded women → WPA's one-family-member policy favoured men → Social Security excluded domestic and agricultural workers.
p2: Widespread opposition to married women working → Aid to Dependent Children reinforced motherhood over independence → New Deal assumed a male breadwinner throughout.
p3: Black women excluded by white-administered Southern relief → Mexican American women vulnerable to deportation → rural women had least access of all.

front: What were the strengths of women's position by 1932?
p1: 19th Amendment (1920) after 50 years → League of Women Voters educated voters → women 44% of undergraduates by 1930 → ERA introduced (1923).
p2: American Birth Control League → 222 clinics by 1941 → WTUL advocating for working women → flapper culture loosened urban middle-class norms.
p3: Some women in state legislatures and Congress → Women's Bureau (1920) in the Department of Labor → League of Women Voters active.

front: What were the weaknesses of women's position by 1932?
p1: Suffrage limited: only 1/3 voted in the 1920s → Black women faced voter suppression in the South → ERA rejected repeatedly → women earned half male wages.
p2: Depression (1929): women first targeted for job losses → public opinion strongly opposed married women working → Comstock Laws still in force.
p3: Structural inequality: gender pay gap entrenched → professional barriers to law, medicine and business remained strong → cultural pressure for the domestic sphere intensified by the Depression.

front: How did women benefit from the New Deal?
p1: WPA employed 400,000 women by 1938 → many women's first formal wage labour of the Depression.
p2: FLSA (1938): minimum wage, 44-hour week, child labour ban → first-time protections for many women workers.
p3: NLRB, FLSA and Social Security gave a legal framework later equal pay campaigns built on → BUT the gender pay gap persisted at the time.

front: What was universal about women's experience during the New Deal?
p1: All women faced 80% public opposition to married women working (1936 Gallup) → all excluded from higher-paying jobs and political decision-making → Depression devastated all women.
p2: WPA employed women across racial lines, though segregated → Aid to Dependent Children reached single mothers across races, though unequally.
p3: CCC excluded all women → gender pay gap universal, whether white professional or Black domestic worker → all women seen as secondary earners.

front: How different were women's experiences during the New Deal?
p1: By race: Black women excluded from most relief programmes → domestic and agricultural workers excluded from Social Security → Mexican American women vulnerable to deportation.
p2: By class: middle-class women accessed professional roles (Perkins, Roosevelt, Allen) → working-class women concentrated in excluded sectors → WPA employed women in gender-segregated, lower-paid roles.
p3: By location: rural women of every race had least access → urban women accessed WPA and CIO unions → Southern women most affected by discrimination from local white administrators.

front: What was the impact of WWII on women's employment?
p1: 6 million women entered the workforce in WWII → by 1944, 1 in 4 married women working → Rosie the Riveter → Lanham Act (1941): federal childcare funding for working mothers.
p2: 75% wanted to remain employed after WWII, unlike post-WWI → entered industrial, professional and technical roles previously closed.
p3: BUT 2 million lost jobs in 1946 as men returned → GI Bill mainly benefited male veterans → women's undergraduate share fell from 40% (1920) to 30% (1950).

front: What was the significance of Dr Spock and the post-war housewife ideal?
p1: Dr Spock's Baby and Child Care (1946): 23 million copies → argued mothers in the workplace were a source of childhood instability.
p2: Cold War conformity: domestic sphere framed as patriotic duty → GI Bill reinforced the male-breadwinner model → women's undergraduate share fell 40% (1920) to 30% (1950).
p3: Reinforced the 1950s suburban housewife as the dominant ideal → Friedan's Feminine Mystique (1963) later named the damage.

front: What was the Kennedy Commission on the Status of Women (1961)?
p1: Kennedy Commission (1961): chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt → first federal body to document systematic sex discrimination.
p2: Led directly to the Equal Pay Act (1963), the first federal law prohibiting pay discrimination by sex → women earned 59¢ per $1 in 1963.
p3: First time federal government formally acknowledged gender discrimination → broke from the assumption that inequality was natural → set the legislative agenda for the next decade.

front: What were the key ideas of the Feminine Mystique (1963)?
p1: Friedan identified 'the problem with no name' → college-educated suburban housewives' profound unhappiness in their prescribed domestic role → called marriage a 'comfortable concentration camp'.
p2: Argument: post-war society trapped women in domesticity, constructed by advertisers, Freudian psychologists and women's magazines → kept women out of public life and consuming domestic products.
p3: 3 million copies in 3 years → Friedan co-founded NOW (1966) → launched second-wave feminism.

front: What was the significance of NOW?
p1: NOW (1966): founded by Friedan and other feminists → Miss America protest (1968) crowned a pig, symbolically rejecting objectification.
p2: Lobbied for Title VII (employment discrimination) enforcement, Title IX (education discrimination), ERA ratification and reproductive rights.
p3: Women's Strike for Equality (1970): 50,000+ marched in New York for equal pay, childcare and abortion rights → NOW had 40,000 members by 1972, a mainstream organisation exerting real pressure.

front: What was the significance of the Civil Rights Act (1964) Title VII?
p1: Title VII (1964): prohibited employment discrimination by sex → Alice Paul had lobbied for its inclusion → late addition but became one of the most powerful legal tools.
p2: EEOC established to enforce → initial resistance: chairman called the sex provision a 'fluke' → NOW (1966) formed partly to pressure the EEOC.
p3: Opened professional roles to women → women could sue employers → with the Equal Pay Act (1963), the foundation for economic equality claims.

front: What was the significance of second-wave and radical feminism?
p1: Second-wave feminism went beyond suffrage → demanded economic, social and cultural equality → NOW (1966), Women's Strike for Equality (1970), Ms Magazine (1972).
p2: Radical feminism: Miss America protest (1968) crowned a pig → Burial of True Womanhood at Arlington National Cemetery (1968) → 'The Feminists' called for abolition of marriage.
p3: Tensions: radical feminism energised the movement but alienated moderates → sparked backlash → Schlafly's Stop ERA mobilised around fear of its implications.

front: What was the significance of the Pill (1960)?
p1: Pill approved by FDA (1960): 6 million women using it by 1965 → unprecedented autonomy over reproduction → birth rate declined sharply → women could plan careers alongside family.
p2: Separated sex from reproduction → contributed to the sexual revolution → challenged traditional gender roles.
p3: Limits: not available to unmarried women until Eisenstadt v Baird (1972) → access unequal across class and race → strong Catholic Church opposition.

front: What were Griswold v Connecticut (1965) and Eisenstadt v Baird (1972)?
p1: Griswold v Connecticut (1965): Supreme Court struck down a state ban on contraceptives for married couples → right to marital privacy.
p2: Eisenstadt v Baird (1972): extended contraceptive rights to unmarried individuals → completed the right to contraception regardless of marital status.
p3: Both built on the legal foundation Sanger had fought for since 1916 → overturned 90 years of Comstock Laws' reproductive suppression.

front: What was the significance of Title IX (1972)?
p1: Title IX (1972): prohibited gender discrimination in federally funded education → universities had to provide equal opportunities in sports, academics and admissions.
p2: Women's college sports teams rose from 16,000 (1972) to 50,000 by 1978 → female athletic scholarships created → transformed women's participation in sport.
p3: Limits: inconsistent enforcement → excluded private institutions → did not address pay inequality in teaching → later threatened by Reagan budget cuts.

front: What was the significance of Roe v Wade (1973)?
p1: Roe v Wade (1973): abortion protected under the constitutional right to privacy established in Griswold (1965) → invalidated most state abortion laws.
p2: National Organisation for Repeal of Abortion Laws (1969) had built pressure → with Griswold and Eisenstadt (1972), a complete reproductive rights framework in under a decade.
p3: BUT immediately polarising → National Right to Life Committee formed the same year → Hyde Amendment (1976) restricted federal abortion funding, hitting low-income women most.

front: What was the position of women in organised labour in the early 20th century?
p1: WTUL (1903): first sustained effort to organise women workers → Bread and Roses Strike (1912): 20,000 immigrant women in Lawrence won a 15% pay rise → model of cross-ethnic solidarity.
p2: Triangle Shirtwaist (1911) galvanised the movement, transforming public attitude to women workers and feeding WTUL's safety campaigns.
p3: Limits: AFL consistently excluded women from skilled unions → women concentrated in non-unionised clerical and domestic work → FLSA (1938) excluded domestic workers.

front: How did Black Power advance Black women's position?
p1: Triple oppression of race, gender and class named → foundational for Black feminism → Elaine Brown chaired the Black Panther Party (BPP) → Kathleen Cleaver was BPP spokesperson.
p2: Cultural reclamation: Afro hairstyle rejected Eurocentric beauty standards → Angela Davis and Ella Baker widely recognised → raised healthcare, education and economic opportunity as Black women's concerns.
p3: Women central to survival programmes (day care, food, health) → showed Black women could lead their own struggles → Black feminism emerged as a distinct movement.

front: How did Black Power limit the position of Black women?
p1: Male chauvinism in the BPP: women relegated to typing, cooking and logistics → ideas ignored unless proposed by men → 'revolutionary first, Sister second'.
p2: NOI rejected birth control and criticised women challenging gender roles → Black Power leaders saw feminism as a 'white women's issue' → focus on reclaiming Black masculinity limited gender equality.
p3: Even prominent women faced dismissal: Angela Davis criticised for doing a man's job → serving roles treated as expected subjugation rather than leadership.

front: How did Black Power influence the wider women's movement?
p1: Intersectionality: Black Power highlighted race, gender and class intersections → foundational for Black feminism and mainstream feminist theory → radical feminism adopted Panther-inspired direct action.
p2: NOW pushed, slowly, to incorporate racial justice → Davis, Brown and Cleaver brought revolutionary spirit → Fannie Lou Hamer showed Black women could lead their own struggles.
p3: Fish-ins, occupations and confrontational media strategies influenced by Black Power → second-wave feminism more militant because of its example.

front: How limited was Black Power's influence on the women's movement?
p1: NOW and mainstream feminists focused on white middle-class concerns (equal pay, reproductive rights) → often sidelining the unique struggles of Black women.
p2: Black Power leaders dismissed feminism as 'a white movement' → focus on reclaiming Black masculinity limited integration of women's concerns.
p3: Radical feminism's rise had multiple drivers: Betty Friedan, the pill and second-wave feminism were equally significant → Black Power was one influence among several.

front: What were Phyllis Schlafly's arguments against the ERA?
p1: ERA would eliminate protective legislation that benefited women: minimum wage laws, workplace safety protections, exemptions from heavy labour.
p2: ERA would force women into military combat roles and unisex public facilities → framed as attacking women's distinct social position, not just legal rights.
p3: ERA would destroy the traditional family → framed feminism as a threat to domestic life, not a campaign for legal equality.

front: What was the political polarisation over abortion after Roe v Wade?
p1: Before Roe, abortion was not a major partisan issue → both parties contained pro-choice and anti-abortion politicians.
p2: After Roe: National Right to Life Committee (1973) → Republican Party adopted an anti-abortion platform → Reagan (1981-89) opposed abortion rights and made conservative Supreme Court appointments.
p3: By 1992 abortion was the primary gender issue splitting parties → Planned Parenthood v Casey (1992) allowed state restrictions → showed Roe's ongoing vulnerability.

front: What was the ERA and why did it fail?
p1: First proposed by Alice Paul (1923) → reintroduced every Congress for 50 years without success.
p2: Finally passed Congress (1972) → a constitutional guarantee that equal rights could not be denied on account of sex.
p3: Schlafly's Stop ERA mobilised conservative women → only 35 of 38 states ratified by the 1982 deadline → later gains (Equal Pay Act, Title VII, Title IX) rest on statute, not the Constitution.

front: What was the impact of the anti-feminist backlash?
p1: Schlafly's Stop ERA built an evangelical Christian women's base → fed the Moral Majority (1979), which opposed abortion, ERA and feminism as a package.
p2: National Right to Life Committee (1973) formed in response to Roe → Hyde Amendment (1976) restricted federal abortion funding → class dimension: wealthier women could still access abortion privately.
p3: Created a lasting political realignment: abortion and gender politics became entrenched partisan dividing lines, shaping Republican platforms into the 1990s and beyond.

front: What were the political rights of women by 1992?
p1: Year of the Woman: 24 women elected to the House (11%), 6 to the Senate → O'Connor first female Supreme Court Justice (1981) → Ferraro first female VP nominee (1984).
p2: 55% of women voted vs 49% of men → participation exceeded men's → BUT ERA unratified, with no constitutional guarantee of sex equality → Roe under threat from Casey (1992).
p3: Women's Political Caucus (1971) had built the pipeline → BUT only 10% of elected federal officials were women → glass ceiling in politics as well as the workplace.

front: What was the social position of women by 1992?
p1: 60% of women employed, working mothers the norm → average 2.2 children, lowest since the 19th century → women outpacing men in graduation: 84% vs 78%.
p2: 40% of law and medical degrees → Title IX (1972) transformed girls' sports and education → BUT domestic violence still underreported and underprosecuted → rape shield laws still developing.
p3: Roe v Wade (1973) gave reproductive rights → BUT Hyde Amendment (1976) restricted funding → Planned Parenthood v Casey (1992) allowed state restrictions → rights left fragile.

front: What was the economic position of women by 1992?
p1: Women 40% of the workforce → 75¢ per $1 (up from 59¢ in 1963) → glass ceiling: only 10% of senior management were women.
p2: Equal Pay Act (1963) + Title VII (1964) gave the legal foundation → EEOC enforced → BUT enforcement slow and glass ceiling entrenched → CLUW (1974) pushed unions on equal pay.
p3: Deindustrialisation hit women in manufacturing → but service sector growth created new employment → women dominated healthcare, education and retail, often lower-paid.

front: What forms did racial violence take during Reconstruction (1865-77)?
p1: Memphis and New Orleans riots (1866): white mobs attacked Black residents and their supporters → dozens to 200 killed.
p2: Colfax Massacre (1873): white supremacists killed over 100 African Americans in Louisiana to stop them voting and holding office → federal government failed to help.
p3: Violence at poll booths, lynching and destruction of Black organisations → intimidation continued after 1877 against those trying to register to vote.

front: What was the significance of Prohibition for women (1919-33)?
p1: 18th Amendment (1919) established Prohibition → a victory for temperance advocates like the WCTU (300,000+ members), working alongside the Anti-Saloon League (1893).
p2: Divided women by class: middle-class women saw alcohol as destroying families, but many working-class and immigrant women resented the moral imposition → Molly Pitcher Club (1922) campaigned against it, citing organised crime and brewery job losses.
p3: 21st Amendment (1933) repealed Prohibition → marked the waning influence of women-led temperance campaigns as government moved away from moral reform.
